checkpoints: Category listings cache at the response/entry-point tier — since the page is identical for every visitor, this cuts the whole pipeline, not just the DB query.
Category listings get an hours-long TTL, because they only change a few times a day.
Product detail gets its own cache entry with a shorter TTL than category listings, because merchant edits happen more often than category changes.
Search results cannot share one response-tier entry across users — they cache at the logic tier keyed on normalized (sorted/defaulted/trimmed) parameters, with the shortest TTL of the three surfaces.
Every parameter that changes the output (category id, product id, normalized search params) must be encoded in the cache key, and nothing personalized is ever cached under a shared key.
Each write path has an explicit invalidation contract: a product update clears its own detail key AND every category-listing key it belongs to; a category change clears that category's listing keys.

A popular key expiring under heavy traffic causes a stampede — many concurrent requests MISS at once and hit the database simultaneously — mitigated with a single-flight rebuild or refreshing the key just before it expires, keeping the database as the one source of truth.
Orders/Payments goes in the relational store because money needs ACID — strict invariants, foreign-key constraints, multi-row transactions — and this store is the source of truth for money.
Catalog goes in the document store because its attributes vary per product type and evolve weekly, so schema flexibility avoids a migration per attribute change.
Activity feed goes in the document store because it's append-only, high-volume, and always read by a single key, which fits document locality.
Each module hides its own storage engine behind a contract, and ids stay opaque across the boundary — no direct join across the two stores.
Every data item has exactly one owning module / one declared source of truth, independent of which engine stores it.
Nothing transacts across the two engines: a purchase commits in the relational store first (that is the truth), then the feed entry propagates asynchronously and can visibly lag by a few seconds.

Splitting into two engines (polyglot persistence) is justified only by genuine divergence in needs between the sub-domains, not by default, and it charges a real price — two operational surfaces plus eventual consistency to manage at every crossing point.
User-profile is one-to-one, so the foreign key sits on one declared owning side only.
Order-line item is one-to-many, so the foreign key sits on the many side (each line item stores its own orderId) — an order row has nowhere to hold an unbounded list of item ids.
Which side holds the foreign key is dictated by cardinality, not by preference.
Student-course is many-to-many, so neither side can hold a single foreign-key column — an intermediate table storing (studentId, courseId) pairs is required instead.
The ORM generates and maintains that intermediate join table automatically from the declared relation, with no hand-written entity needed.
When hydrated, a one-to-one/many-to-one relation arrives as a single nested object, while a one-to-many/many-to-many relation arrives as an array.
Getting the cardinality declaration wrong makes the resulting schema itself wrong, which no ORM can fix after the fact.
The symptom — a count that comes out lower than the true number of events, only under heavy parallel traffic, with code that is individually correct — is the signature of a read-modify-write race.

The interleaving: request A reads `likes: 100`, request B reads `likes: 100` before A has written anything back, A computes 101 and writes it, and B also computes 101 from its own stale read and writes it — one tap is silently lost, with no exception ever firing to point at it.
The vulnerable window is entirely between the client's read and its write-back.
A sequential five-tap test never opens that window, which is why the bug looked fixed until real concurrency arrived.

The fix is to stop reading the value into application code at all: send the database a server-side atomic increment operator instead (MongoDB's `$inc`; the same idea shows up as `Update.inc(...)` in Spring Data MongoDB, `Builders<T>.Update.Inc(...)` on the .NET driver, and a `$inc` document on the Go driver), so the database itself performs read+add+write as one indivisible step per document.
There is no window left for a second request to interleave into, because every write to a single document is atomic.
Verification has to match the failure mode: fire N genuinely concurrent increments (not a loop of sequential calls) and assert the counter lands on exactly N.

The atomicity guarantee stops at the document — if the same action also had to stay consistent with a document elsewhere (e.g. decrementing stock in one collection while creating an order in another), a single-document atomic operator cannot cover that; that needs a multi-document transaction or an optimistic-concurrency-control scheme instead.

The right question is never "which engine is faster" but what shape the data has and what consistency level the business needs — the real trade-off axis is ACID versus BASE/eventual consistency, not speed, and that axis is what can turn a wholesale migration into a hard-to-undo mistake.
Dismantle the benchmark: speed depends on the workload — a small key-based document read can be fast, but a multi-table JOIN/aggregate query is SQL's home turf.
An end-to-end latency number measured over the network is not an engine-power benchmark; it only measures one workload at one point in time.
Data that is genuinely relational and needs constraints/ACID transactions — financial transactions, orders — must stay on SQL, because a money transaction stopping halfway is unacceptable.
Data that is self-contained, read by key, frequently evolving in shape, and needing horizontal scale — catalogs, logs, flexible profiles — is document territory.
Polyglot persistence (running both engines) is justified only when different sub-domains genuinely have different shape/consistency needs, not run "just in case".

The accompanying cost of polyglot persistence: no transaction spans both engines, so a write succeeding on one side and failing on the other requires an outbox pattern or saga/compensation mechanism to handle the divergence.

The correct process is to enumerate real queries and required consistency levels, benchmark against the actual workload, then migrate selectively if warranted — a wholesale migration driven by one number risks losing data that matters.
Steelman raw SQL first: it gives exact control over the query and a transparent execution plan, with no wondering what JOIN the framework generated.
Without a mapping layer, each relation (passport, toys, owners) becomes its own query plus hand-written stitching code — boilerplate that must be revisited every time the schema changes.
Manual foreign-key tracking is exactly where a typo desyncs a toy from its cat — a correctness risk that hand-rolled relations introduce.
Looping per row to fetch each relation by hand is precisely how an N+1 query pattern gets written, not introduced by accident.

The mapping layer's real value: cardinality (1-1, 1-N, N-N) is declared once as entity metadata (@OneToOne/@OneToMany/@ManyToMany plus foreign-key ownership), from which the ORM generates the JOINs and hydrates flat rows into nested objects/arrays.
Assigning cat onto a new toy and saving writes the foreign key catId underneath automatically, with no manual key management.

Honest limit: the ORM is only a translation layer, not the model itself — declaring the wrong cardinality or the wrong eager/lazy choice still yields a wrong schema or a slow N+1 query regardless of the ORM.

Dropping to raw SQL is a legitimate, selective call for complex reporting/aggregate queries or a hot path proven inefficient by measurement — default to the mapping layer for CRUD and relation traversal, and reach for raw SQL as a scalpel, not a blanket policy.
Core principle: the document model stores data in the shape it will be read in — this is the underlying reason embed-vs-reference is a usage-driven decision, not a fixed rule.
The embed-vs-reference decision must be driven by how each piece of data is read, written, shared, and how fast it grows — not a hard rule applied to every case.
Case (a): spec attributes and tags are bounded, exclusively owned by the product, and always read alongside it — so embed, giving a single read and a single atomic update.

Case (b): activity history grows unbounded per event (risking the 16MB document size limit) and is queried independently by other dashboards — so reference it into its own collection keyed by customer id.
Cost of referencing: reads become multiple queries or a join-style lookup, and cross-document updates lose single-document atomicity.
That atomicity loss is acceptable here because each history entry is an append-only fact that is never updated back.
Drift warning: embedding shared data purely to trade for read speed risks updates made in many places rotting out of sync over time — follow the real read/write pattern, not a default choice.

A root query that returns N rows followed by N nearly-identical child queries differing only by a foreign-key parameter is the signature of the N+1 query pattern — the shape alone identifies it before any code is read.

ORMs such as TypeORM do not hydrate relations by default: a plain call like `catRepository.find()` returns only the root rows, leaving a nested collection such as `cat.toys` unset unless the query explicitly asks for that relation.

Looping over the root rows and issuing one relation query per row turns what should be a single round-trip into N round-trips to the database, so the query count — and therefore latency — grows linearly with the number of rows instead of staying constant.

The fix is to request the relation on the root query itself (for example `relations: ["toys"]`, or a query-builder `leftJoinAndSelect`), which makes the ORM generate one JOIN-based query and hydrate every row's nested array in a single pass.
With the relation declared on the root query, the total query count stays at exactly 1 no matter how many cats exist, so response time no longer scales with row count.

Eager-loading every relation on every query is an overcorrection: an endpoint that never reads a given relation still pays for the extra JOIN and the hydrated data it doesn't use, so which relations to load should be decided per endpoint rather than applied as a blanket default.

Confirming the fix means re-running with query logging enabled and checking two things: the query count dropped from N+1 to exactly 1, and latency stays flat when comparing a small dataset (e.g. 10 rows) against a much larger one (e.g. 1000 rows).

Response-tier caching such as NestJS's CacheInterceptor stores the entire HTTP response at the entry point, and on a cache hit it returns that stored value directly without ever invoking the handler again — pipes, parameter decorators like @CurrentUser(), and the service logic simply don't run for a hit.

`@CacheKey("dashboard")` is a static string literal, so every caller hitting the endpoint maps to the exact same Redis key regardless of who is making the request — there is nothing in the key that distinguishes one user from another.

The first request that misses the cache runs the real handler for one specific user, and Redis stores that user's exact DashboardDto under the shared key; every other request within the TTL window then gets that same cached payload back, exposing one user's personalized data to everyone else.

Clean auth logs are consistent with this bug rather than evidence against it: JWT validation and @CurrentUser() resolution only execute on the cache miss that populates the entry, so a correct session on that one request says nothing about who the cached response gets served to afterward.

The intermittency tracks the cache TTL directly — each expiry forces a fresh miss, and whichever user's request happens to land first after that expiry becomes the new cached payload for the next window, so the leaked identity keeps shifting on a fixed cycle rather than staying constant.

A response-tier cache is only safe for output that is identical for every caller; the moment an endpoint's output varies by an authenticated identity, that identity has to be part of the cache key, or a personalized response stored under a shared key is a data leak by construction.

Fixing it means either keying the cache per identity — overriding `trackBy` on a custom CacheInterceptor to build a key like `dashboard:${user.id}` and accepting a fragmented hit rate — or dropping caching out of the response tier altogether and caching only the shared, non-personal data at the logic/service level while recomputing the personalized part on every call.

Correct verification reproduces the incident with two different authenticated sessions inside a single TTL window and confirms each now receives only their own data, inspects the cache keyspace (e.g. Redis `KEYS`) to confirm entries are per-user or the response-tier entry is gone, and adds a regression test that exercises two users back to back.

Embedding an array or nested object inside a parent document is the right default only when the data is bounded, belongs to the parent, and is read together with it — an activityLog that gains one entry per login, view, and click has no upper bound, so the document keeps growing toward MongoDB's 16MB document-size limit.

Because activityLog is embedded on Customer, every read or write of the customer document carries the entire activity history along with it, even when the caller only needs the customer's basic fields like email.

An append-only, ever-growing event log belongs in its own referenced collection (e.g. a CustomerActivity schema keyed by customerId) rather than nested inside the parent, so it can be inserted and queried independently and the parent document stays small.

A document database enforces no shape on a schemaless field — Mongoose's `@Prop({ type: Object })` (or Spring's Map, .NET's Dictionary, Go's map[string]any) accepts anything — so declaring metadata that way with no DTO or class-validator check anywhere in the PR means the schema hasn't disappeared, it has simply moved into the application layer where nobody wrote it.

Skipping that application-level validation means literally any structure can be persisted into metadata, since the database itself will accept and store an arbitrary object without complaint or rejection.

findByEmail is called on every login but the email field has no index declared and no explicit schema.index({ email: 1 }) call, so the query runs as a full collection scan; it looks fast today only because the sample collection is small, and scan time grows roughly linearly with the number of customers.

Tests passing and the code running fine locally proves nothing about how it behaves once real usage accumulates, since small sample data hides both unbounded array growth and the cost of a missing index on a hot query path like login.

A code review should tie each objection to a concrete future failure mode and read/write pattern rather than only naming the problem, explicitly separating what works on today's data from what survives growth, and proposing a fix alongside each finding.

Concerns like these should be substantiated rather than merely asserted from opinion — a seeded-growth test can check the resulting document size against the size limit, and an explain()/execution-plan check run before and after adding the index can prove a full collection scan was actually eliminated.
